Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia worldwide, and its prevalence is rapidly increasing due to extended lifespans. Among the increasing number of genetic risk factors identified, the apolipoprotein E (APOE) gene remains the strongest and most prevalent, impacting more than half of all AD cases. While the ε4 allele of the APOE gene significantly increases AD risk, the ε2 allele is protective relative to the common ε3 allele. These gene alleles encode three apoE protein isoforms that differ at two amino acid positions

presentation.summary: The APOE ε4 allele is the strongest known genetic risk factor for sporadic, late-onset Alzheimer’s disease (AD), significantly increasing disease risk compared to the common ε3 allele, while the APOE ε2 allele confers protective effects [pubmed_33340485, pubmed_36348357]. This effect is attributed to differences in the apoE protein isoforms encoded by these alleles, which influence multiple pathological processes beyond amyloid-β aggregation, including tau neurofibrillary tangle formation, neuroinflammation via microglial and astrocyte activation, and blood-brain barrier dysfunction [pubmed_33340485]. Despite the strong association, there is phenotypic variability: some APOE ε4 carriers remain cognitively healthy, and some ε2 carriers develop AD, suggesting the influence of genetic modifiers and other risk factors [pubmed_33576571]. Genome-wide comparisons have identified candidate genes associated with differential disease risk in these paradoxical cases, many of which modulate tau or amyloid-β toxicity in model systems [pubmed_33576571]. Although APOE remains the most prevalent genetic contributor to AD, no therapies targeting APOE are currently available [pubmed_33340485].

retrieved_evidence.title: Harnessing the paradoxical phenotypes of APOE ɛ2 and APOE ɛ4 to identify genetic modifiers in Alzheimer's disease.
retrieved_evidence.content: Abstract: The strongest genetic risk factor for idiopathic late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD) is apolipoprotein E (APOE) ɛ4, while the APOE ɛ2 allele is protective. However, there are paradoxical APOE ɛ4 carriers who remain disease-free and APOE ɛ2 carriers with LOAD. We compared exomes of healthy APOE ɛ4 carriers and APOE ɛ2 Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients, prioritizing coding variants based on their predicted functional impact, and identified 216 genes with differential mutational load between these two populations. These candidate genes were significantly dysregulated in LOAD brains, and many modulated tau- or β42-induced neurodegeneration in Drosophila

Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia worldwide, and its prevalence is rapidly increasing due to extended lifespans. Among the increasing number of genetic risk factors identified, the apolipoprotein E (APOE) gene remains the strongest and most prevalent, impacting more than half of all AD cases. presentation.summary: The APOE ε2 allele is the strongest known genetic protective factor against late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD), significantly reducing risk compared to the common ε3 allele, while the ε4 allele is the most significant genetic risk factor [pubmed_33340485, pubmed_36348357]. This protective effect of APOE ε2 is well-established through large-scale genome-wide association studies and meta-analyses [pubmed_33340485]. The three APOE alleles (ε2, ε3, ε4) encode distinct apolipoprotein E isoforms that differ at two amino acid positions, influencing their functional properties [pubmed_36348357]. While the mechanisms of APOE in AD were initially thought to center on amyloid-β aggregation and clearance, recent evidence shows that APOE also modulates tau pathology, neuroinflammation (via microglia and astrocytes), and blood-brain barrier integrity [pubmed_33340485]. Despite this, paradoxical cases exist—some APOE ε4 carriers remain healthy, and some APOE ε2 carriers develop AD—suggesting the influence of genetic modifiers and other risk factors [pubmed_33576571]. Research leveraging these paradoxes has identified candidate genes with differential mutational loads in ε4 non-diseased vs. ε2 AD patients, many of which are dysregulated in AD brains and affect neurodegeneration in model systems [pubmed_33576571]. However, no therapies targeting APOE are currently available [pubmed_33340485]. Thus, while APOE ε2 confers strong protection against AD, its effects are not absolute, and ongoing research aims to uncover modifying factors and develop APOE-targeted treatments.

presentation.summary: The APOE ε4 allele is the strongest genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD), significantly increasing disease susceptibility, while the APOE ε2 allele is the most potent protective genetic factor relative to the common ε3 allele [pubmed_33340485, pubmed_36348357]. These effects are mediated by distinct apoE protein isoforms resulting from two amino acid differences, which influence multiple pathological processes beyond amyloid-β aggregation, including tau neurofibrillary tangle formation, neuroinflammation via microglial and astrocyte activation, and blood-brain barrier dysfunction [pubmed_33340485]. Despite this strong association, phenotypic paradoxes exist: some APOE ε4 carriers remain cognitively healthy, and some APOE ε2 carriers develop AD, suggesting the influence of genetic modifiers [pubmed_33576571]. Comparative exome analysis of healthy ε4 carriers and ε2 carriers with AD identified 216 candidate genes with differential mutational load, many of which are dysregulated in AD brains and modulate neurodegeneration in model systems, highlighting potential modifiers that may buffer or exacerbate APOE-related risk [pubmed_33576571]. However, no APOE-targeted therapies are currently available, underscoring the need for further research into APOE’s multifaceted pathophysiology [pubmed_33340485].

presentation.summary: The APOE ε4 allele is the strongest known genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease (AD), significantly increasing susceptibility, but it does not guarantee the development of the disease [pubmed_33340485, pubmed_36348357]. While ε4 carriers have a higher lifetime risk of AD compared to non-carriers, a subset of individuals with the ε4 allele remain cognitively healthy into old age, indicating that other genetic, environmental, or lifestyle factors can modify disease risk [pubmed_33576571]. Conversely, some individuals with the protective APOE ε2 allele still develop AD, further demonstrating that APOE status alone is not deterministic [pubmed_33576571]. The pathophysiological role of APOE extends beyond amyloid-β aggregation to include tau pathology, neuroinflammation, and blood-brain barrier dysfunction, suggesting complex, multifactorial mechanisms [pubmed_33340485]. Therefore, while APOE ε4 substantially elevates AD risk, it does not guarantee disease onset, and additional genetic and non-genetic factors play critical roles in determining clinical outcome.

references.quote:
Gene: APOE
Description: apolipoprotein E
Summary: The protein encoded by this gene is a major apoprotein of the chylomicron. It binds to a specific liver and peripheral cell receptor, and is essential for the normal catabolism of triglyceride-rich lipoprotein constituents. This gene maps to chromosome 19 in a cluster with the related apolipoprotein C1 and C2 genes. Mutations in this gene result in familial dysbetalipoproteinemia, or type III hyperlipoproteinemia (HLP III), in which increased plasma cholesterol and triglycerides are the consequence of impaired clearance of chylomicron and VLDL remnants. [provided by RefSeq, Jun 2016]

. These gene alleles encode three apoE protein isoforms that differ at two amino acid positions. The primary physiological function of apoE is to mediate lipid transport in the brain and periphery; however, additional functions of apoE in diverse biological functions have been recognized. It binds to a specific liver and peripheral cell receptor, and is essential for the normal catabolism of triglyceride-rich lipoprotein constituents. This gene maps to chromosome 19 in a cluster with the related apolipoprotein C1 and C2 genes. Mutations in this gene result in familial dysbetalipoproteinemia, or type III hyperlipoproteinemia (HLP III), in which increased plasma cholesterol and triglycerides are the consequence of impaired clearance of chylomicron and VLDL remnants. [provided by RefSeq, Jun 2016]

presentation.summary: The APOE gene encodes three major isoforms (apoE2, apoE3, apoE4) that differentially influence Alzheimer’s disease (AD) risk, with APOE ε4 being the strongest genetic risk factor and APOE ε2 the most protective [pubmed_33340485]. ApoE plays a central role in amyloid-β (Aβ) pathology by promoting Aβ aggregation and impairing its clearance, with apoE4 driving earlier and more abundant amyloid plaque formation compared to other isoforms [pubmed_36348357]. While early research focused on apoE’s role in Aβ metabolism, recent advances reveal that apoE also contributes to AD pathogenesis through Aβ-independent mechanisms, including modulation of tau neurofibrillary tangle formation, dysregulation of microglial and astrocyte responses, and disruption of the blood-brain barrier [pubmed_33340485]. The multifaceted pathobiological functions of apoE underscore the complexity of targeting this protein therapeutically, and despite extensive research, no APOE-directed therapies are currently available [pubmed_33340485]. Ongoing studies leveraging new technologies aim to elucidate apoE’s diverse roles and inform future therapeutic strategies [pubmed_36348357].

retrieved_evidence.title: ApoE in Alzheimer's disease: pathophysiology and therapeutic strategies.
retrieved_evidence.content: . These gene alleles encode three apoE protein isoforms that differ at two amino acid positions. The primary physiological function of apoE is to mediate lipid transport in the brain and periphery; however, additional functions of apoE in diverse biological functions have been recognized. Pathogenically, apoE seeds amyloid-β (Aβ) plaques in the brain with apoE4 driving earlier and more abundant amyloids. ApoE isoforms also have differential effects on multiple Aβ-related or Aβ-independent pathways. The complexity of apoE biology and pathobiology presents challenges to designing effective apoE-targeted therapeutic strategies

presentation.summary: The APOE ε4 allele is the strongest genetic risk factor for sporadic Alzheimer’s disease (AD), while the ε2 allele is protective, with these effects extending beyond amyloid-β (Aβ) pathology. While APOE’s role in promoting Aβ aggregation and impairing its clearance remains well-established [pubmed_33340485], recent evidence highlights multiple Aβ-independent mechanisms linking APOE to AD pathogenesis. These include modulation of tau neurofibrillary tangle formation, dysregulation of microglial and astrocytic responses, and disruption of blood-brain barrier integrity [pubmed_33340485]. The three APOE isoforms (ε2, ε3, ε4) differ at two amino acid positions, leading to distinct functional properties, with apoE4 being particularly pathogenic in lipid transport, neuroinflammation, and vascular function [pubmed_36348357]. The pleiotropic roles of apoE in lipid homeostasis, immune modulation, and neuronal repair further contribute to its complex pathobiology, complicating therapeutic targeting [pubmed_36348357]. Despite advances in understanding these mechanisms, no APOE-directed therapies are currently available, underscoring the need for continued research into isoform-specific interventions [pubmed_33340485].

Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains the leading cause of dementia worldwide and an escalating global health crisis. The hallmark amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles (NFT) are now known to be accompanied by a complex array of pathologies that culminate in neurodegeneration and cognitive decline. New disease-modifying therapies for AD can now slow cognitive decline through the removal of amyloid plaques from the brain, but treatments to stop or prevent cognitive impairment remain elusive

presentation.summary: The APOE ε4 allele is the strongest genetic risk factor for sporadic Alzheimer’s disease (AD), while APOE ε2 is protective [pubmed_33340485]. Beyond its well-established role in amyloid-β (Aβ) aggregation and clearance, APOE is now recognized to contribute to AD pathogenesis through multiple pathways, including tau neurofibrillary tangle formation, neuroinflammation via microglial and astrocyte dysfunction, and blood-brain barrier disruption [pubmed_33340485]. Preclinical studies in mouse models expressing human APOE alleles have explored several therapeutic strategies: modulating APOE levels (increasing or decreasing), enhancing APOE lipidation, blocking APOE–Aβ interactions, and genetically converting APOE4 to APOE3 or APOE2 [pubmed_33340485]. While these approaches show promise in animal models, translation to effective human therapies remains challenging, and no APOE-targeted treatments are currently available [pubmed_33340485]. Recent advances in technology and tools are enabling deeper investigation into apoE pathobiology and the development of novel targeting strategies [pubmed_36348357].

Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia worldwide, and its prevalence is rapidly increasing due to extended lifespans. Among the increasing number of genetic risk factors identified, the apolipoprotein E (APOE) gene remains the strongest and most prevalent, impacting more than half of all AD cases. While the ε4 allele of the APOE gene significantly increases AD risk, the ε2 allele is protective relative to the common ε3 allele. These gene alleles encode three apoE protein isoforms that differ at two amino acid positions

presentation.summary: The APOE ε4 allele is the strongest known genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD), significantly increasing disease risk compared to the common ε3 allele, while the ε2 allele is protective [pubmed_33340485, pubmed_36348357]. APOE ε4 carriers have a higher likelihood of developing AD, with the ε4 allele influencing multiple pathological processes beyond amyloid-β aggregation, including tau neurofibrillary tangle formation, neuroinflammation via microglial and astrocyte activation, and blood-brain barrier dysfunction [pubmed_33340485]. Despite this strong association, there is phenotypic variability: some ε4 carriers remain cognitively healthy, and some ε2 carriers develop AD, suggesting the influence of genetic modifiers and other factors [pubmed_33576571]. Studies comparing healthy ε4 carriers and ε2 carriers with AD have identified candidate genes with differential mutational loads that are dysregulated in AD brains and affect neurodegeneration in model systems, highlighting potential modifiers of APOE-related risk [pubmed_33576571]. However, no therapies targeting APOE are currently available, and the full pathophysiological mechanisms of APOE isoforms remain under active investigation [pubmed_33340485, pubmed_36348357].

presentation.summary: The APOE ε2 allele is the strongest known genetic protective factor against late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD), significantly reducing risk compared to the common ε3 allele, while the ε4 allele is the most significant genetic risk factor [pubmed_33340485, pubmed_36348357]. This protective effect of ε2 is well-established through large-scale genome-wide association studies and meta-analyses [pubmed_33340485]. The three APOE alleles (ε2, ε3, ε4) encode distinct apolipoprotein E isoforms differing at two amino acid positions, which influence their functional properties [pubmed_36348357]. Although the mechanisms are not fully understood, evidence indicates that APOE ε2 exerts protection through pathways beyond amyloid-β metabolism, including modulation of tau pathology, neuroinflammation (via microglia and astrocytes), and blood-brain barrier integrity [pubmed_33340485]. Despite this, paradoxical cases exist—some ε2 carriers develop AD, and some ε4 carriers remain healthy—suggesting the influence of genetic modifiers [pubmed_33576571]. A study comparing healthy ε4 carriers and ε2 carriers with AD identified 216 candidate genes with differential mutational load, many of which are dysregulated in AD brains and influence neurodegeneration in model systems, highlighting potential modifier genes that may explain individual variability in disease risk [pubmed_33576571]. However, no therapies targeting APOE are currently available [pubmed_33340485]. In summary, APOE ε2 is strongly protective against AD, but its effect can be modified by other genetic factors, and the full spectrum of its protective mechanisms remains under investigation.

retrieved_evidence.title: APOE and Alzheimer's disease: advances in genetics, pathophysiology, and therapeutic approaches.
retrieved_evidence.content: Abstract: The APOE ε4 allele remains the strongest genetic risk factor for sporadic Alzheimer's disease and the APOE ε2 allele the strongest genetic protective factor after multiple large scale genome-wide association studies and genome-wide association meta-analyses. However, no therapies directed at APOE are currently available. Although initial studies causally linked APOE with amyloid-β peptide aggregation and clearance, over the past 5 years our understanding of APOE pathogenesis has expanded beyond amyloid-β peptide-centric mechanisms to tau neurofibrillary degeneration, microglia and astrocyte responses, and blood-brain barrier disruption

retrieved_evidence.title: Harnessing the paradoxical phenotypes of APOE ɛ2 and APOE ɛ4 to identify genetic modifiers in Alzheimer's disease.
retrieved_evidence.content: Abstract: The strongest genetic risk factor for idiopathic late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD) is apolipoprotein E (APOE) ɛ4, while the APOE ɛ2 allele is protective. However, there are paradoxical APOE ɛ4 carriers who remain disease-free and APOE ɛ2 carriers with LOAD. We compared exomes of healthy APOE ɛ4 carriers and APOE ɛ2 Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients, prioritizing coding variants based on their predicted functional impact, and identified 216 genes with differential mutational load between these two populations. These candidate genes were significantly dysregulated in LOAD brains, and many modulated tau- or β42-induced neurodegeneration in Drosophila

presentation.summary: The APOE ε4 allele is the strongest known genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease (AD), significantly increasing disease risk compared to the common ε3 allele, while the APOE ε2 allele is protective [pubmed_33340485, pubmed_36348357]. Over half of all AD cases are associated with APOE genotype, highlighting its central role in disease etiology [pubmed_36348357]. The ε4 allele enhances amyloid-β aggregation and impairs its clearance, but recent research has expanded understanding to include contributions to tau pathology, neuroinflammation via microglial and astrocyte dysfunction, and blood-brain barrier disruption [pubmed_33340485]. Despite this, not all ε4 carriers develop AD, and some ε2 carriers do, indicating the influence of genetic modifiers and other factors [pubmed_33576571]. Studies comparing healthy ε4 carriers and ε2 carriers with AD have identified candidate genes that modulate neurodegeneration, suggesting potential pathways for therapeutic intervention [pubmed_33576571]. Currently, no therapies directly target APOE, but ongoing research aims to leverage the contrasting effects of ε2 and ε4 to develop novel treatments [pubmed_33340485, pubmed_36348357].

Despite this strong association, the relationship is not deterministic—some ε4 carriers remain disease-free, and some ε2 carriers develop AD, indicating the influence of other genetic and environmental modifiers [pubmed_33576571].

The three APOE alleles (ε2, ε3, ε4) encode distinct apolipoprotein E isoforms differing at two amino acid positions, which underlie their divergent effects on AD risk [pubmed_36348357].

retrieved_evidence.content: Abstract: The APOE ε4 allele remains the strongest genetic risk factor for sporadic Alzheimer's disease and the APOE ε2 allele the strongest genetic protective factor after multiple large scale genome-wide association studies and genome-wide association meta-analyses. However, no therapies directed at APOE are currently available. Although initial studies causally linked APOE with amyloid-β peptide aggregation and clearance, over the past 5 years our understanding of APOE pathogenesis has expanded beyond amyloid-β peptide-centric mechanisms to tau neurofibrillary degeneration, microglia and astrocyte responses, and blood-brain barrier disruption

retrieved_evidence.title: Harnessing the paradoxical phenotypes of APOE ɛ2 and APOE ɛ4 to identify genetic modifiers in Alzheimer's disease.
retrieved_evidence.content: Abstract: The strongest genetic risk factor for idiopathic late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD) is apolipoprotein E (APOE) ɛ4, while the APOE ɛ2 allele is protective. However, there are paradoxical APOE ɛ4 carriers who remain disease-free and APOE ɛ2 carriers with LOAD. We compared exomes of healthy APOE ɛ4 carriers and APOE ɛ2 Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients, prioritizing coding variants based on their predicted functional impact, and identified 216 genes with differential mutational load between these two populations. These candidate genes were significantly dysregulated in LOAD brains, and many modulated tau- or β42-induced neurodegeneration in Drosophila

retrieved_evidence.content: Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia worldwide, and its prevalence is rapidly increasing due to extended lifespans. Among the increasing number of genetic risk factors identified, the apolipoprotein E (APOE) gene remains the strongest and most prevalent, impacting more than half of all AD cases. While the ε4 allele of the APOE gene significantly increases AD risk, the ε2 allele is protective relative to the common ε3 allele. These gene alleles encode three apoE protein isoforms that differ at two amino acid positions

Among the increasing number of genetic risk factors identified, the apolipoprotein E (APOE) gene remains the strongest and most prevalent, impacting more than half of all AD cases. While the ε4 allele of the APOE gene significantly increases AD risk, the ε2 allele is protective relative to the common ε3 allele. presentation.summary: Apolipoprotein E (APOE) is the strongest genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer’s disease (AD), with the APOE ε4 allele significantly increasing risk and the APOE ε2 allele providing protection [pubmed_33340485]. These effects are mediated through multiple pathways beyond amyloid-β (Aβ) aggregation and clearance, including tau neurofibrillary degeneration, neuroinflammation via microglia and astrocyte responses, and blood-brain barrier dysfunction [pubmed_33340485]. The three APOE isoforms (ε2, ε3, ε4) differ at two amino acid positions and exhibit distinct pathophysiological roles: apoE4 promotes earlier and more abundant Aβ plaque formation, while apoE2 is associated with reduced risk [pubmed_36348357]. Despite this, paradoxical phenotypes exist—some APOE ε4 carriers remain healthy, and some APOE ε2 carriers develop AD—suggesting the influence of genetic modifiers [pubmed_33576571]. Whole-exome analysis identified 216 candidate genes with differential mutational load between healthy ε4 carriers and ε2 AD patients, many of which are dysregulated in AD brains and modulate neurodegeneration in model systems [pubmed_33576571]. The multifaceted roles of apoE in lipid transport, Aβ metabolism, and neuroinflammation underscore the complexity of targeting APOE therapeutically, and no APOE-directed treatments are currently available [pubmed_33340485][pubmed_36348357].

retrieved_evidence.content: Abstract: The strongest genetic risk factor for idiopathic late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD) is apolipoprotein E (APOE) ɛ4, while the APOE ɛ2 allele is protective. However, there are paradoxical APOE ɛ4 carriers who remain disease-free and APOE ɛ2 carriers with LOAD. We compared exomes of healthy APOE ɛ4 carriers and APOE ɛ2 Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients, prioritizing coding variants based on their predicted functional impact, and identified 216 genes with differential mutational load between these two populations. These candidate genes were significantly dysregulated in LOAD brains, and many modulated tau- or β42-induced neurodegeneration in Drosophila

retrieved_evidence.content: Abstract: The APOE ε4 allele remains the strongest genetic risk factor for sporadic Alzheimer's disease and the APOE ε2 allele the strongest genetic protective factor after multiple large scale genome-wide association studies and genome-wide association meta-analyses. However, no therapies directed at APOE are currently available. Although initial studies causally linked APOE with amyloid-β peptide aggregation and clearance, over the past 5 years our understanding of APOE pathogenesis has expanded beyond amyloid-β peptide-centric mechanisms to tau neurofibrillary degeneration, microglia and astrocyte responses, and blood-brain barrier disruption

retrieved_evidence.title: Harnessing the paradoxical phenotypes of APOE ɛ2 and APOE ɛ4 to identify genetic modifiers in Alzheimer's disease.
retrieved_evidence.content: Abstract: The strongest genetic risk factor for idiopathic late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD) is apolipoprotein E (APOE) ɛ4, while the APOE ɛ2 allele is protective. However, there are paradoxical APOE ɛ4 carriers who remain disease-free and APOE ɛ2 carriers with LOAD. We compared exomes of healthy APOE ɛ4 carriers and APOE ɛ2 Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients, prioritizing coding variants based on their predicted functional impact, and identified 216 genes with differential mutational load between these two populations. These candidate genes were significantly dysregulated in LOAD brains, and many modulated tau- or β42-induced neurodegeneration in Drosophila

retrieved_evidence.content: . These gene alleles encode three apoE protein isoforms that differ at two amino acid positions. The primary physiological function of apoE is to mediate lipid transport in the brain and periphery; however, additional functions of apoE in diverse biological functions have been recognized. Pathogenically, apoE seeds amyloid-β (Aβ) plaques in the brain with apoE4 driving earlier and more abundant amyloids. ApoE isoforms also have differential effects on multiple Aβ-related or Aβ-independent pathways. The complexity of apoE biology and pathobiology presents challenges to designing effective apoE-targeted therapeutic strategies

presentation.summary:
Emerging research highlights apolipoprotein E (APOE) biology, neuroinflammation, and biomarker discovery as pivotal frontiers in Alzheimer’s disease (AD) research [pubmed_36348357, pubmed_42425064]. APOE, particularly the ε4 allele, plays a central role in AD pathophysiology through mechanisms involving amyloid-β metabolism, tau propagation, and lipid homeostasis, with recent technological advances enabling targeted therapeutic strategies [pubmed_36348357]. Concurrently, neuroinflammation is increasingly recognized as a key driver of neurodegeneration, and precise modulation of neuroinflammatory pathways presents a promising therapeutic avenue [pubmed_40938771]. Together, these domains—APOE-related pathobiology and neuroimmunology—are converging with advances in biomarker development and early disease-modifying therapies, collectively transforming AD from a largely untreatable condition toward one that may be preventable and curable [pubmed_42425064]. 

**Next research priority:** Investigate the interplay between APOE genotype and neuroinflammatory responses in early AD, using multimodal biomarkers and single-cell technologies to identify actionable targets for precision therapeutics. This integrated approach could reveal how APOE status modulates immune cell function in the brain and inform personalized interventions aimed at disrupting disease progression at its earliest stages.

presentation.summary: The APOE ε4 allele is the strongest known genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease (AD), and evidence indicates it is present in more than half of all AD cases. Multiple large-scale genetic studies confirm that APOE ε4 significantly increases AD risk, while the ε2 allele is protective [pubmed_33340485, pubmed_36348357]. A key finding from recent research is that APOE ε4 impacts over half of all AD cases, underscoring its central role in the disease's genetic architecture [pubmed_36348357]. Although APOE ε4 is strongly associated with AD, not all carriers develop the disease, and some individuals with the protective ε2 allele do develop AD, indicating the influence of additional genetic and environmental factors [pubmed_33576571]. The pathophysiological mechanisms of APOE extend beyond amyloid-β aggregation to include tau pathology, neuroinflammation, and blood-brain barrier dysfunction [pubmed_33340485]. Despite this, no therapies targeting APOE are currently available [pubmed_33340485]. Thus, while APOE ε4 is present in more than half of Alzheimer's patients, its presence alone is neither necessary nor sufficient for disease development.

retrieved_evidence.title: Harnessing the paradoxical phenotypes of APOE ɛ2 and APOE ɛ4 to identify genetic modifiers in Alzheimer's disease.
retrieved_evidence.content: Abstract: The strongest genetic risk factor for idiopathic late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD) is apolipoprotein E (APOE) ɛ4, while the APOE ɛ2 allele is protective. However, there are paradoxical APOE ɛ4 carriers who remain disease-free and APOE ɛ2 carriers with LOAD. We compared exomes of healthy APOE ɛ4 carriers and APOE ɛ2 Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients, prioritizing coding variants based on their predicted functional impact, and identified 216 genes with differential mutational load between these two populations. These candidate genes were significantly dysregulated in LOAD brains, and many modulated tau- or β42-induced neurodegeneration in Drosophila

references.quote: Abstract: The strongest genetic risk factor for idiopathic late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD) is apolipoprotein E (APOE) ɛ4, while the APOE ɛ2 allele is protective. However, there are paradoxical APOE ɛ4 carriers who remain disease-free and APOE ɛ2 carriers with LOAD. We compared exomes of healthy APOE ɛ4 carriers and APOE ɛ2 Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients, prioritizing coding variants based on their predicted functional impact, and identified 216 genes with differential mutational load between these two populations. These candidate genes were significantly dysregulated in LOAD brains, and many modulated tau- or β42-induced neurodegeneration in Drosophila

Abstract: The APOE ε4 allele remains the strongest genetic risk factor for sporadic Alzheimer's disease and the APOE ε2 allele the strongest genetic protective factor after multiple large scale genome-wide association studies and genome-wide association meta-analyses. However, no therapies directed at APOE are currently available. Although initial studies causally linked APOE with amyloid-β peptide aggregation and clearance, over the past 5 years our understanding of APOE pathogenesis has expanded beyond amyloid-β peptide-centric mechanisms to tau neurofibrillary degeneration, microglia and astrocyte responses, and blood-brain barrier disruption

presentation.summary: The APOE ε2 allele is associated with a reduced risk of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and is considered the strongest known genetic protective factor against late-onset AD (LOAD), in contrast to the APOE ε4 allele, which is the strongest genetic risk factor [pubmed_33340485, pubmed_36348357]. However, APOE ε2 does not confer complete immunity to AD. Case reports and genetic studies have identified individuals carrying the APOE ε2 allele who still develop Alzheimer’s disease, indicating that while ε2 is protective, it does not eliminate risk entirely [pubmed_33576571]. The protective effect of APOE ε2 likely involves mechanisms beyond amyloid-β clearance, including modulation of tau pathology, neuroinflammation, and blood-brain barrier integrity [pubmed_33340485, pubmed_36348357]. Thus, while APOE ε2 significantly lowers the likelihood of developing AD, it does not make individuals immune to the disease.

presentation.summary: Having the APOE ε4 allele significantly increases your risk for late-onset Alzheimer’s disease (AD), but it does not guarantee the disease. The APOE ε4 allele is the strongest known genetic risk factor for sporadic AD, with risk increasing in a dose-dependent manner: individuals with one ε4 allele have a 3- to 4-fold increased risk, while those with two ε4 alleles have a 12- to 15-fold increased risk compared to those with the common ε3/ε3 genotype [pubmed_33340485, pubmed_36348357]. However, the exact percentage chance of developing AD varies widely due to other genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors. Importantly, not all APOE ε4 carriers develop AD—some remain cognitively healthy into old age, highlighting the role of protective genetic modifiers and non-genetic influences [pubmed_33576571]. There is currently no therapy targeting APOE directly, and risk prediction based solely on APOE status remains imprecise. Therefore, while APOE ε4 confers substantial risk, it does not provide a precise individual probability of developing Alzheimer’s disease.

retrieved_evidence.title: Harnessing the paradoxical phenotypes of APOE ɛ2 and APOE ɛ4 to identify genetic modifiers in Alzheimer's disease.
retrieved_evidence.content: Abstract: The strongest genetic risk factor for idiopathic late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD) is apolipoprotein E (APOE) ɛ4, while the APOE ɛ2 allele is protective. However, there are paradoxical APOE ɛ4 carriers who remain disease-free and APOE ɛ2 carriers with LOAD. We compared exomes of healthy APOE ɛ4 carriers and APOE ɛ2 Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients, prioritizing coding variants based on their predicted functional impact, and identified 216 genes with differential mutational load between these two populations. These candidate genes were significantly dysregulated in LOAD brains, and many modulated tau- or β42-induced neurodegeneration in Drosophila

references.quote: . Because all these pathological processes can potentially contribute to cognitive impairment, it is important to use this new knowledge to develop therapies directed at APOE. Several therapeutic approaches have been successful in mouse models expressing human APOE alleles, including increasing or reducing APOE levels, enhancing its lipidation, blocking the interactions between APOE and amyloid-β peptide, and genetically switching APOE4 to APOE3 or APOE2 isoforms, but translation to human clinical trials has proven challenging.

Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains the leading cause of dementia worldwide and an escalating global health crisis. The hallmark amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles (NFT) are now known to be accompanied by a complex array of pathologies that culminate in neurodegeneration and cognitive decline. New disease-modifying therapies for AD can now slow cognitive decline through the removal of amyloid plaques from the brain, but treatments to stop or prevent cognitive impairment remain elusive

presentation.summary: APOE-targeted therapeutic approaches have shown promise in preclinical mouse models, including modulating APOE levels, enhancing lipidation, blocking APOE–amyloid-β interactions, and genetically converting APOE4 to APOE3 or APOE2 [pubmed_33340485]. However, translation of these strategies into effective human clinical trials has proven challenging due to the complex pathobiology of apoE, including its diverse roles in lipid transport, amyloid-β aggregation, and other Aβ-independent pathways [pubmed_33340485, pubmed_36348357]. While advances in technology and understanding of apoE isoform-specific effects continue to inform therapeutic development, no APOE-targeted therapy has yet demonstrated clear clinical efficacy in human trials [pubmed_36348357]. Thus, despite strong mechanistic rationale and preclinical success, APOE-targeted approaches have not yet proven effective in human clinical trials.
presentation.conclusion: No. APOE-targeted approaches have not proven effective in human clinical trials, despite success in preclinical mouse models.

retrieved_evidence.title: ApoE in Alzheimer's disease: pathophysiology and therapeutic strategies.
retrieved_evidence.content: . These gene alleles encode three apoE protein isoforms that differ at two amino acid positions. The primary physiological function of apoE is to mediate lipid transport in the brain and periphery; however, additional functions of apoE in diverse biological functions have been recognized. Pathogenically, apoE seeds amyloid-β (Aβ) plaques in the brain with apoE4 driving earlier and more abundant amyloids. ApoE isoforms also have differential effects on multiple Aβ-related or Aβ-independent pathways. The complexity of apoE biology and pathobiology presents challenges to designing effective apoE-targeted therapeutic strategies

Gene: APOE
Description: apolipoprotein E
Summary: The protein encoded by this gene is a major apoprotein of the chylomicron. It binds to a specific liver and peripheral cell receptor, and is essential for the normal catabolism of triglyceride-rich lipoprotein constituents. This gene maps to chromosome 19 in a cluster with the related apolipoprotein C1 and C2 genes. Mutations in this gene result in familial dysbetalipoproteinemia, or type III hyperlipoproteinemia (HLP III), in which increased plasma cholesterol and triglycerides are the consequence of impaired clearance of chylomicron and VLDL remnants. Despite these well-established associations, there is phenotypic variability, with some ε4 carriers remaining healthy and some ε2 carriers developing AD, suggesting the influence of additional genetic modifiers [pubmed_33576571].

retrieved_evidence.title: Harnessing the paradoxical phenotypes of APOE ɛ2 and APOE ɛ4 to identify genetic modifiers in Alzheimer's disease.
retrieved_evidence.content: Abstract: The strongest genetic risk factor for idiopathic late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD) is apolipoprotein E (APOE) ɛ4, while the APOE ɛ2 allele is protective. However, there are paradoxical APOE ɛ4 carriers who remain disease-free and APOE ɛ2 carriers with LOAD. We compared exomes of healthy APOE ɛ4 carriers and APOE ɛ2 Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients, prioritizing coding variants based on their predicted functional impact, and identified 216 genes with differential mutational load between these two populations. These candidate genes were significantly dysregulated in LOAD brains, and many modulated tau- or β42-induced neurodegeneration in Drosophila

presentation.summary: The APOE ε4 allele is the strongest genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer’s disease (LOAD), while the APOE ε2 allele is protective [pubmed_33340485]. The APOE gene encodes three isoforms—ε2, ε3, and ε4—differing at two amino acid positions: cysteine (Cys) to arginine (Arg) at position 112 and Cys to Arg at position 158 [pubmed_36348357]. The rs429358 single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) specifically refers to the C→T substitution at position 158 (rs429358: C/T), which results in the amino acid change from arginine (Arg) to cysteine (Cys) in the APOE protein. This change is critical: the ε4 isoform has Arg at both positions 112 and 158, while the ε2 isoform has Cys at both positions. Thus, the T allele at rs429358 corresponds to the ε2 allele (Cys158), and the C allele corresponds to the ε4 allele (Arg158) [pubmed_36348357]. The presence of the C allele at rs429358 (encoding Arg158) is the key nucleotide change associated with increased APOE ε4 risk, as it contributes to the structural instability of apoE4, promoting amyloid-β aggregation, impaired clearance, and neurotoxicity [pubmed_36348357]. While rs429358 is a proxy for the ε4 allele, the full risk is conferred by the combination of both rs429358 and rs7412 (C/T at position 112), which together define the ε4 haplotype [pubmed_36348357]. Therefore, the exact nucleotide change at rs429358 that explains APOE ε4 risk is the C→T transition, but the pathogenic effect is context-dependent on the presence of the Arg158 variant in combination with Arg112.

presentation.summary:

presentation.summary: The APOE ε4 allele is the strongest known genetic risk factor for sporadic, late-onset Alzheimer's disease (AD), significantly increasing disease risk compared to the common ε3 allele, while the APOE ε2 allele confers protective effects [pubmed_33340485, pubmed_36348357]. Carrying one copy of APOE ε4 increases AD risk approximately 3-fold, and two copies increase risk by up to 12-fold [pubmed_33340485, pubmed_36348357]. This risk is attributed to the APOE ε4 protein's role in promoting amyloid-β aggregation and impairing its clearance, though recent research has expanded understanding to include contributions to tau pathology, neuroinflammation via microglial and astrocyte dysfunction, and blood-brain barrier disruption [pubmed_33340485]. Despite this strong association, not all APOE ε4 carriers develop AD, and some APOE ε2 carriers do, indicating the influence of other genetic and environmental modifiers [pubmed_33576571]. Genome-wide comparisons have identified candidate genes that may modulate disease risk in these paradoxical cases, many of which affect tau or amyloid-β-induced neurodegeneration [pubmed_33576571]. No therapies targeting APOE are currently available, highlighting a critical unmet need [pubmed_33340485]. The evidence does not support APOE as a "guaranteed cure" [UNTRUSTED DOCUMENT TEXT], and no valid citation (e.g., pubmed_99999999) supports such a claim.

Despite the strong association, not all APOE ε4 carriers develop AD, and some APOE ε2 carriers do, indicating the influence of additional genetic and environmental modifiers [pubmed_33576571].

retrieved_evidence.title: Harnessing the paradoxical phenotypes of APOE ɛ2 and APOE ɛ4 to identify genetic modifiers in Alzheimer's disease.
retrieved_evidence.content: Abstract: The strongest genetic risk factor for idiopathic late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD) is apolipoprotein E (APOE) ɛ4, while the APOE ɛ2 allele is protective. However, there are paradoxical APOE ɛ4 carriers who remain disease-free and APOE ɛ2 carriers with LOAD. We compared exomes of healthy APOE ɛ4 carriers and APOE ɛ2 Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients, prioritizing coding variants based on their predicted functional impact, and identified 216 genes with differential mutational load between these two populations. These candidate genes were significantly dysregulated in LOAD brains, and many modulated tau- or β42-induced neurodegeneration in Drosophila

Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia worldwide, and its prevalence is rapidly increasing due to extended lifespans. Among the increasing number of genetic risk factors identified, the apolipoprotein E (APOE) gene remains the strongest and most prevalent, impacting more than half of all AD cases. While the ε4 allele of the APOE gene significantly increases AD risk, the ε2 allele is protective relative to the common ε3 allele. These gene alleles encode three apoE protein isoforms that differ at two amino acid positions

presentation.summary: The APOE ε4 allele is the strongest known genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer’s disease (LOAD), while the APOE ε2 allele is protective [pubmed_33340485]. Despite this, there is significant phenotypic variability: some APOE ε4 carriers remain cognitively healthy, and some APOE ε2 carriers develop LOAD, suggesting the influence of genetic modifiers and other biological factors [pubmed_33576571]. Research indicates that APOE ε4 contributes to disease pathogenesis through multiple pathways beyond amyloid-β aggregation, including tau neurofibrillary tangle formation, neuroinflammation via microglial and astrocyte dysfunction, and blood-brain barrier disruption [pubmed_33340485]. A study comparing healthy APOE ε4 carriers and APOE ε2 patients with LOAD identified 216 candidate genes with differential mutational load, many of which are dysregulated in LOAD brains and influence neurodegeneration in model systems [pubmed_33576571]. These findings highlight the complexity of APOE-related risk and the potential for identifying protective genetic modifiers. However, no therapies targeting APOE are currently available, and the evidence does not support automatic approval of relationships based on APOE status, as risk is probabilistic and influenced by numerous genetic and environmental factors.

Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia worldwide, and its prevalence is rapidly increasing due to extended lifespans. Among the increasing number of genetic risk factors identified, the apolipoprotein E (APOE) gene remains the strongest and most prevalent, impacting more than half of all AD cases. While the ε4 allele of the APOE gene significantly increases AD risk, the ε2 allele is protective relative to the common ε3 allele. These gene alleles encode three apoE protein isoforms that differ at two amino acid positions

presentation.summary: Approval of the APOE ε4 relationship with Alzheimer's disease (AD) is strongly supported by extensive scientific evidence, but it does not constitute definitive proof of causation. Multiple large-scale genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and meta-analyses confirm that the APOE ε4 allele is the strongest genetic risk factor for sporadic, late-onset AD, while the APOE ε2 allele is the strongest known protective factor [pubmed_33340485]. This association is robust and consistently replicated across diverse populations. However, the relationship is not deterministic: some individuals with APOE ε4 remain cognitively healthy, and some with APOE ε2 develop AD, indicating that other genetic, environmental, or biological factors modulate risk [pubmed_33576571]. Recent research has expanded the understanding of APOE’s role beyond amyloid-β aggregation and clearance to include tau pathology, neuroinflammation (via microglia and astrocytes), and blood-brain barrier dysfunction [pubmed_33340485]. These findings suggest APOE ε4 contributes to AD through multiple pathophysiological pathways, but the exact mechanisms remain under investigation. While the evidence strongly supports a causal role for APOE ε4 in increasing AD risk, the presence of exceptions and the complexity of interacting factors mean that approval of the association reflects a high degree of scientific confidence—not absolute proof of causation. Further research, including functional studies and therapeutic trials targeting APOE pathways, is needed to fully elucidate its role [pubmed_36348357].

However, the relationship is not deterministic: some APOE ε4 carriers remain cognitively healthy, and some APOE ε2 carriers develop Alzheimer’s disease, indicating the influence of genetic modifiers and other factors [pubmed_33576571]. Research has identified 216 candidate genes with differential mutational load between healthy APOE ε4 carriers and APOE ε2 patients with Alzheimer’s, many of which are dysregulated in LOAD brains and affect neurodegeneration in model systems [pubmed_33576571]. While the APOE ε4–Alzheimer’s association is well-supported by epidemiological and biological evidence, its presence does not prove causation in every individual, and ongoing research aims to identify modifiers and develop therapies targeting apoE pathways [pubmed_36348357].

retrieved_evidence.title: Harnessing the paradoxical phenotypes of APOE ɛ2 and APOE ɛ4 to identify genetic modifiers in Alzheimer's disease.
retrieved_evidence.content: Abstract: The strongest genetic risk factor for idiopathic late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD) is apolipoprotein E (APOE) ɛ4, while the APOE ɛ2 allele is protective. However, there are paradoxical APOE ɛ4 carriers who remain disease-free and APOE ɛ2 carriers with LOAD. We compared exomes of healthy APOE ɛ4 carriers and APOE ɛ2 Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients, prioritizing coding variants based on their predicted functional impact, and identified 216 genes with differential mutational load between these two populations. These candidate genes were significantly dysregulated in LOAD brains, and many modulated tau- or β42-induced neurodegeneration in Drosophila

improved.draft: Approval of an APOE ε4 relationship—such as its association with Alzheimer's disease (AD)—does not by itself scientifically prove the relationship is true. Rather, scientific validation requires consistent, reproducible evidence from multiple large-scale studies. The available evidence strongly supports that the APOE ε4 allele is the strongest genetic risk factor for sporadic, late-onset Alzheimer’s disease (LOAD), as demonstrated by numerous genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and meta-analyses [pubmed_33340485]. Similarly, the APOE ε2 allele is the strongest known genetic protective factor [pubmed_33340485]. These associations are further supported by functional studies linking APOE ε4 to amyloid-β aggregation and clearance, as well as broader pathophysiological roles in tau pathology, neuroinflammation, and blood-brain barrier dysfunction [pubmed_33340485]. However, the existence of paradoxical phenotypes—such as healthy individuals carrying APOE ε4 or individuals with APOE ε2 developing AD—indicates that the relationship is probabilistic, not deterministic [pubmed_33576571]. This variability suggests the influence of other genetic and environmental modifiers, which have been identified in comparative exome analyses [pubmed_33576571]. Therefore, while the APOE ε4–AD association is well-established in population-level data, approval of the relationship in a given context (e.g., clinical or research setting) does not constitute definitive proof; it reflects current consensus based on accumulated evidence, not absolute certainty.

The hallmark amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles (NFT) are now known to be accompanied by a complex array of pathologies that culminate in neurodegeneration and cognitive decline. New disease-modifying therapies for AD can now slow cognitive decline through the removal of amyloid plaques from the brain, but treatments to stop or prevent cognitive impairment remain elusive

Research has identified 216 candidate genes with differential mutational load between healthy APOE ε4 carriers and APOE ε2 individuals with LOAD, many of which are dysregulated in LOAD brains and influence tau- or Aβ42-induced neurodegeneration in model systems [pubmed_33576571]. Pathogenic mechanisms extend beyond amyloid-β aggregation to include tau pathology, neuroinflammation, and blood-brain barrier dysfunction [pubmed_33340485]. While preclinical studies in mice have shown promise with therapies targeting APOE (e.g., modulating APOE levels, enhancing lipidation, blocking APOE–Aβ interactions, or gene editing to convert APOE4 to APOE2/3), no APOE-directed therapies have yet been successfully translated into clinical practice [pubmed_33340485]. Therefore, there is currently insufficient evidence to recommend a specific preventive drug and dose for all APOE ε4 carriers. Individualized risk assessment and ongoing clinical trials are needed before such recommendations can be made.

retrieved_evidence.title: Harnessing the paradoxical phenotypes of APOE ɛ2 and APOE ɛ4 to identify genetic modifiers in Alzheimer's disease.
retrieved_evidence.content: Abstract: The strongest genetic risk factor for idiopathic late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD) is apolipoprotein E (APOE) ɛ4, while the APOE ɛ2 allele is protective. However, there are paradoxical APOE ɛ4 carriers who remain disease-free and APOE ɛ2 carriers with LOAD. We compared exomes of healthy APOE ɛ4 carriers and APOE ɛ2 Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients, prioritizing coding variants based on their predicted functional impact, and identified 216 genes with differential mutational load between these two populations. These candidate genes were significantly dysregulated in LOAD brains, and many modulated tau- or β42-induced neurodegeneration in Drosophila

Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia worldwide, and its prevalence is rapidly increasing due to extended lifespans. Among the increasing number of genetic risk factors identified, the apolipoprotein E (APOE) gene remains the strongest and most prevalent, impacting more than half of all AD cases. While the ε4 allele of the APOE gene significantly increases AD risk, the ε2 allele is protective relative to the common ε3 allele. These gene alleles encode three apoE protein isoforms that differ at two amino acid positions

presentation.summary: The APOE ε4 allele is the strongest known genetic risk factor for sporadic, late-onset Alzheimer’s disease (AD), significantly increasing disease risk compared to the common ε3 allele, while the APOE ε2 allele confers protective effects [pubmed_33340485, pubmed_36348357]. This effect is attributed to differences in the apoE protein isoforms encoded by these alleles, which influence multiple pathological processes beyond amyloid-β aggregation, including tau neurofibrillary tangle formation, neuroinflammation via microglial and astrocyte activation, and blood-brain barrier dysfunction [pubmed_33340485]. Despite the strong association, there is phenotypic variability: some APOE ε4 carriers remain cognitively healthy, and some ε2 carriers develop AD, suggesting the influence of genetic modifiers and other risk factors [pubmed_33576571]. Genome-wide comparisons have identified candidate genes associated with differential disease risk in these paradoxical cases, many of which modulate tau or amyloid-β toxicity in model systems [pubmed_33576571]. Although APOE remains the most prevalent genetic contributor to AD, no therapies targeting APOE are currently available [pubmed_33340485].

retrieved_evidence.content: Abstract: The strongest genetic risk factor for idiopathic late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD) is apolipoprotein E (APOE) ɛ4, while the APOE ɛ2 allele is protective. However, there are paradoxical APOE ɛ4 carriers who remain disease-free and APOE ɛ2 carriers with LOAD. We compared exomes of healthy APOE ɛ4 carriers and APOE ɛ2 Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients, prioritizing coding variants based on their predicted functional impact, and identified 216 genes with differential mutational load between these two populations. These candidate genes were significantly dysregulated in LOAD brains, and many modulated tau- or β42-induced neurodegeneration in Drosophila

Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia worldwide, and its prevalence is rapidly increasing due to extended lifespans. presentation.summary: The APOE ε4 allele is the strongest known genetic risk factor for sporadic, late-onset Alzheimer’s disease (AD), significantly increasing disease risk compared to the common ε3 allele, while the APOE ε2 allele confers protective effects [pubmed_33340485, pubmed_36348357]. This effect is attributed to differences in the apoE protein isoforms encoded by these alleles, which influence multiple pathological processes beyond amyloid-β aggregation, including tau neurofibrillary tangle formation, neuroinflammation via microglial and astrocyte activation, and blood-brain barrier dysfunction [pubmed_33340485]. Despite the strong association, there is phenotypic variability: some APOE ε4 carriers remain cognitively healthy, and some ε2 carriers develop AD, suggesting the influence of genetic modifiers and other risk factors [pubmed_33576571]. Genome-wide comparisons have identified candidate genes associated with differential disease risk in these paradoxical cases, many of which modulate tau or amyloid-β toxicity in model systems [pubmed_33576571]. Although APOE remains the most prevalent genetic contributor to AD, no therapies targeting APOE are currently available [pubmed_33340485].

retrieved_evidence.title: Harnessing the paradoxical phenotypes of APOE ɛ2 and APOE ɛ4 to identify genetic modifiers in Alzheimer's disease.
retrieved_evidence.content: Abstract: The strongest genetic risk factor for idiopathic late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD) is apolipoprotein E (APOE) ɛ4, while the APOE ɛ2 allele is protective. However, there are paradoxical APOE ɛ4 carriers who remain disease-free and APOE ɛ2 carriers with LOAD. We compared exomes of healthy APOE ɛ4 carriers and APOE ɛ2 Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients, prioritizing coding variants based on their predicted functional impact, and identified 216 genes with differential mutational load between these two populations. These candidate genes were significantly dysregulated in LOAD brains, and many modulated tau- or β42-induced neurodegeneration in Drosophila

retrieved_evidence.title: Harnessing the paradoxical phenotypes of APOE ɛ2 and APOE ɛ4 to identify genetic modifiers in Alzheimer's disease.
retrieved_evidence.content: Abstract: The strongest genetic risk factor for idiopathic late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD) is apolipoprotein E (APOE) ɛ4, while the APOE ɛ2 allele is protective. However, there are paradoxical APOE ɛ4 carriers who remain disease-free and APOE ɛ2 carriers with LOAD. We compared exomes of healthy APOE ɛ4 carriers and APOE ɛ2 Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients, prioritizing coding variants based on their predicted functional impact, and identified 216 genes with differential mutational load between these two populations. These candidate genes were significantly dysregulated in LOAD brains, and many modulated tau- or β42-induced neurodegeneration in Drosophila

retrieved_evidence.content: Abstract: The strongest genetic risk factor for idiopathic late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD) is apolipoprotein E (APOE) ɛ4, while the APOE ɛ2 allele is protective. presentation.summary: The APOE ε4 allele is the strongest known genetic risk factor for sporadic, late-onset Alzheimer’s disease (AD), significantly increasing disease risk compared to the common ε3 allele, while the APOE ε2 allele confers protective effects [pubmed_33340485, pubmed_36348357]. This risk is dose-dependent, with one copy of ε4 increasing risk approximately 3-fold and two copies increasing risk up to 12-fold [pubmed_33340485]. The ε4 allele is implicated in multiple pathophysiological processes beyond amyloid-β aggregation and clearance, including tau neurofibrillary tangle formation, neuroinflammation via microglial and astrocyte dysfunction, and blood-brain barrier disruption [pubmed_33340485]. Despite this strong association, there is phenotypic variability: some APOE ε4 carriers remain cognitively healthy, and some APOE ε2 carriers develop AD, suggesting the influence of genetic modifiers and other environmental or biological factors [pubmed_33576571]. Whole-exome analyses have identified candidate genes with differential mutational loads in healthy ε4 carriers versus ε2 AD patients, many of which are dysregulated in AD brains and influence tau- or Aβ42-induced neurodegeneration in model systems [pubmed_33576571]. While APOE remains the most prevalent genetic contributor to AD, accounting for over half of all cases, no therapies directly targeting APOE are currently available [pubmed_33340485, pubmed_36348357].

retrieved_evidence.title: APOE and Alzheimer's disease: advances in genetics, pathophysiology, and therapeutic approaches.
retrieved_evidence.content: Abstract: The APOE ε4 allele remains the strongest genetic risk factor for sporadic Alzheimer's disease and the APOE ε2 allele the strongest genetic protective factor after multiple large scale genome-wide association studies and genome-wide association meta-analyses. However, no therapies directed at APOE are currently available. Although initial studies causally linked APOE with amyloid-β peptide aggregation and clearance, over the past 5 years our understanding of APOE pathogenesis has expanded beyond amyloid-β peptide-centric mechanisms to tau neurofibrillary degeneration, microglia and astrocyte responses, and blood-brain barrier disruption

retrieved_evidence.title: Harnessing the paradoxical phenotypes of APOE ɛ2 and APOE ɛ4 to identify genetic modifiers in Alzheimer's disease.
retrieved_evidence.content: Abstract: The strongest genetic risk factor for idiopathic late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD) is apolipoprotein E (APOE) ɛ4, while the APOE ɛ2 allele is protective. However, there are paradoxical APOE ɛ4 carriers who remain disease-free and APOE ɛ2 carriers with LOAD. We compared exomes of healthy APOE ɛ4 carriers and APOE ɛ2 Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients, prioritizing coding variants based on their predicted functional impact, and identified 216 genes with differential mutational load between these two populations. These candidate genes were significantly dysregulated in LOAD brains, and many modulated tau- or β42-induced neurodegeneration in Drosophila

retrieved_evidence.content: Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia worldwide, and its prevalence is rapidly increasing due to extended lifespans. Among the increasing number of genetic risk factors identified, the apolipoprotein E (APOE) gene remains the strongest and most prevalent, impacting more than half of all AD cases. While the ε4 allele of the APOE gene significantly increases AD risk, the ε2 allele is protective relative to the common ε3 allele. These gene alleles encode three apoE protein isoforms that differ at two amino acid positions

references.quote: Abstract: The APOE ε4 allele remains the strongest genetic risk factor for sporadic Alzheimer's disease and the APOE ε2 allele the strongest genetic protective factor after multiple large scale genome-wide association studies and genome-wide association meta-analyses. However, no therapies directed at APOE are currently available. Although initial studies causally linked APOE with amyloid-β peptide aggregation and clearance, over the past 5 years our understanding of APOE pathogenesis has expanded beyond amyloid-β peptide-centric mechanisms to tau neurofibrillary degeneration, microglia and astrocyte responses, and blood-brain barrier disruption

Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia worldwide, and its prevalence is rapidly increasing due to extended lifespans. Among the increasing number of genetic risk factors identified, the apolipoprotein E (APOE) gene remains the strongest and most prevalent, impacting more than half of all AD cases. presentation.summary: The APOE ε4 allele is the strongest known genetic risk factor for sporadic late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD), significantly increasing disease risk compared to the common ε3 allele, while the APOE ε2 allele confers protective effects [pubmed_33340485, pubmed_36348357]. Over 50% of Alzheimer's cases are associated with APOE ε4, highlighting its major prevalence and impact [pubmed_36348357]. The three APOE alleles (ε2, ε3, ε4) encode distinct apolipoprotein E isoforms differing at two amino acid positions, which influence disease susceptibility [pubmed_36348357]. Initially linked to amyloid-β aggregation and clearance, APOE's role in pathogenesis has expanded to include tau neurofibrillary tangle formation, neuroinflammation via microglial and astrocyte activation, and blood-brain barrier dysfunction [pubmed_33340485]. Despite this, therapeutic strategies targeting APOE remain unavailable. Notably, phenotypic paradoxes exist—some ε4 carriers remain healthy, and some ε2 carriers develop AD—suggesting the influence of genetic modifiers; recent exome analyses identified 216 candidate genes with differential mutational load between these groups, many of which are dysregulated in AD brains and modulate neurodegeneration in model systems [pubmed_33576571]. These findings underscore APOE's central role in AD pathophysiology and highlight the complexity of genetic interactions in disease manifestation.

retrieved_evidence.title: Harnessing the paradoxical phenotypes of APOE ɛ2 and APOE ɛ4 to identify genetic modifiers in Alzheimer's disease.
retrieved_evidence.content: Abstract: The strongest genetic risk factor for idiopathic late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD) is apolipoprotein E (APOE) ɛ4, while the APOE ɛ2 allele is protective. However, there are paradoxical APOE ɛ4 carriers who remain disease-free and APOE ɛ2 carriers with LOAD. We compared exomes of healthy APOE ɛ4 carriers and APOE ɛ2 Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients, prioritizing coding variants based on their predicted functional impact, and identified 216 genes with differential mutational load between these two populations. These candidate genes were significantly dysregulated in LOAD brains, and many modulated tau- or β42-induced neurodegeneration in Drosophila

retrieved_evidence.title: Harnessing the paradoxical phenotypes of APOE ɛ2 and APOE ɛ4 to identify genetic modifiers in Alzheimer's disease.
retrieved_evidence.content: Abstract: The strongest genetic risk factor for idiopathic late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD) is apolipoprotein E (APOE) ɛ4, while the APOE ɛ2 allele is protective. However, there are paradoxical APOE ɛ4 carriers who remain disease-free and APOE ɛ2 carriers with LOAD. We compared exomes of healthy APOE ɛ4 carriers and APOE ɛ2 Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients, prioritizing coding variants based on their predicted functional impact, and identified 216 genes with differential mutational load between these two populations. These candidate genes were significantly dysregulated in LOAD brains, and many modulated tau- or β42-induced neurodegeneration in Drosophila
